power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Durations selling sex are key determinants of HIV/STI transmission dynamics and service coverage.
Such durations are usually estimated from cross-sectional surveys of people actively selling sex.
However, cross-sectional surveys are more likely to include individuals selling sex for longer, and survey-reported durations will be right-censored.
Prior works have not adequately addressed these two competing biases.
In this paper, we derive the mathematical relationship between the distribution of durations reported in cross-sectional surveys and the distribution of true durations in the population overall.
These distributions will be identical if true durations are exponentially distributed; otherwise, reported durations will typically underestimate the variance in true durations.
We develop a parametric Bayesian model of this relationship, and apply it to re-analyze aggregate data from a global systematic review.

Our model-estimated average true durations selling sex are significantly shorter than previously published for all regions -e.g. in Africa: 2.1 (95% CI: 1.8-2.5) versus 5.5 years; in Asia: 1.4 (1.2-1.5) versus 2.8-4.0 years.
Shorter average durations then suggest that HIV incidence in sex work could be higher than previously thought, to match the same HIV prevalence data.
Our approach can be applied beyond sex work, to characterize duration distributions for any transient risk/disease state.
Epidemiological studies and healthcare programs are often interested in quantifying distributions of durations, such as durations of transient health states or exposure to risk/protective factors.
Estimates of these distributions can help characterize a population's cumulative exposure [1], and inform inputs to state-transition simulation models [2].
text.formatted: Estimates of these distributions can help characterize a population's cumulative exposure <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>, and inform inputs to state-transition simulation models <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: One prominent example is duration in sex work -selling sex for money or equivalent -reflecting a transient period of elevated risk for acquisition and transmission of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections (STI) due to intersecting structural, behavioural, and biological factors [3] [4] [5].

text.text: While entry into sex work is driven primarily by economic and social instability, exit is further mediated by aging, stable partnering, stigma, and violence [6] [7] [8].
text.formatted: While entry into sex work is driven primarily by economic and social instability, exit is further mediated by aging, stable partnering, stigma, and violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Simulation models of HIV/STI transmission have highlighted how unmet prevention and treatment needs within sex work often drive epidemic emergence and persistence [9] [10] [11].
text.formatted: Simulation models of HIV/STI transmission have highlighted how unmet prevention and treatment needs within sex work often drive epidemic emergence and persistence <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: In such models, rates of exit from sex work are typically defined as the inverse of the mean duration in sex work -e.g. a 5-year mean duration corresponding to a 20% exit rate per year.
If the sex worker population size is approximately stable over time, then exiting sex workers must be replaced by a similar number of entering sex workerse.g. corresponding to 20% "turnover" [12].
text.formatted: If the sex worker population size is approximately stable over time, then exiting sex workers must be replaced by a similar number of entering sex workerse.g. corresponding to 20% "turnover" <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Mean durations in sex work are thus key determinants of HIV/STI epidemiology, and key inputs to transmission models, particularly those aiming to compare the impacts of different prioritized services.

For example, 10% HIV prevalence among sex workers in a context with 1-year mean duration (rapid turnover) suggests a high HIV incidence rate, whereas 10% HIV prevalence in a context with 10-year mean durations (slow turnover) suggests a lower HIV incidence rate, since prevalence has more time to accumulate [12, 13].

Finally, duration in sex work can further influence onward transmission risk, where longer durations theoretically allow more onward transmission following acquisition (in the absence of treatment).
Fazito et al. [14] conducted a global scoping review and regional syntheses of mean duration in sex work, with estimates ranging from 2.8 years in Asia to 12 years in Latin America.

text.text: Indeed, there appears to be uncertainty in general regarding how durations reported in cross-sectional studies relate to true overall durations in sex work.

text.text: Objectives To address this uncertainty and challenges/limitations of existing methods to estimate mean duration in sex work, we sought to: 1.
Derive the mathematical relationship between the distribution of observed durations in sex work sex from cross-sectional studies and the distribution of true durations in sex work overall.

Develop and apply a Bayesian model of this relationship with aggregate data from a single illustrative study [18] and a global scoping review [14], and compare model-estimated mean durations in sex work to previously published estimates.

text.text: The remainder of our paper is structured as follows: In § 2, we clarify some key concepts and assumptions for the work.
In § 3, we derive the mathematical relationship for Objective 1.
In § 4, we develop and apply the Bayesian model for Objective 2.
In § 5, we conclude with discussion of implications and future work.
Assumptions For simplicity, we first assume that periods of sex work have clear start/end points, and that formal sex work can be clearly distinguished from transactional sex.
We also assume that surveys predominantly reach those actively engaged in sex work, despite some survey eligibility criteria including individuals who sold sex anytime in the past year, etc. [3].
text.formatted: We also assume that surveys predominantly reach those actively engaged in sex work, despite some survey eligibility criteria including individuals who sold sex anytime in the past year, etc. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: We further assume that survey participants can accurately report how long they have sold sex -i.e. perfect recall, no social desirability bias.
Finally, we assume that all populations are at equilibrium, e.g. rates of entering/exiting sex work are stable over time.
Who exactly are we talking about?
Before continuing, it is helpful to distinguish two populations: individuals who will ever sell sex in their lifetime, and individuals who are actively selling sex.

The former "source population" is the target sample for method 1 in [14], and tends to include more individuals who sell sex for shorter durations; the latter "active population" (a subset of the source population) is the target sample for methods 2 and 3 in [14], and tends to include more individuals who sell sex for longer durations.

In this paper, we have clarified several concepts and challenges relevant to characterizing the distribution of durations in sex work from cross-sectional data.

First, we distinguished between "source" and "active" populations, with the active population being a length-biased subset of the source population, where the probability of being active is proportional to total duration in sex work.
Second, we reiterated the familiar implications of randomly censored durations, which halves the mean duration.

We combined the above to derive the exact mathematical relationship between the distribution of censored durations among the active population and the distribution of total durations among the source population, which we showed to be equal if durations are Exponentially distributed.

We then developed a parametric Bayesian model of this relationship to infer the distribution of total durations among the source population from aggregate data on censored durations among the active population.
Applying this model to data from a previous global systematic review [14], we inferred significantly shorter mean durations across multiple regions.

Limitations Our work has several limitations.
First, we did not model any gaps (temporary breaks) in sex work.
Many estimates of sex work duration are derived from the difference between respondents' current age and the age they report first selling sex, which implicitly ignores such gaps.
Respondents may also report "duration in sex work" in this way when asked directly, especially since unsuccessful attempts to exit sex work can be stigmatized [8].

text.text: The distribution of durations in sex work is a key determinant of HIV/STI dynamics and an essential input to HIV/STI transmission models.
Such durations are commonly reported in cross-sectional studies, where they are subject to two competing biases: length-biased sampling (increases the mean) and censoring (decreases the mean).

The former bias, omitted from prior work, is likely stronger, such that the mean duration reported in cross-sectional studies actually overestimates rather than underestimates the "true" mean duration.
Methods herein also support inference of the complete distribution of "true" durations, given a complete distribution of reported durations.
Notably, these methods can be applied to characterize the distribution of durations beyond sex work, such as for transient health states, or periods of exposure to risk/protective factors.
